title: Genghis Khan Spares the Archer Who Shot His Horse
text:
Around 1201 the young Mongol leader Temujin, not yet called Genghis Khan, fought a battle against the Tayichiud, a rival clan. During the fighting an archer on a hillside shot an arrow that hit Temujin's horse, a prized war horse, in the neck.

The Secret History of the Mongols, the Mongols' own thirteenth-century account, tells what happened after Temujin won. A young man named Jirgoadai, who had fought for the Tayichiud, came to submit. Temujin asked who had shot his horse from the hill.

Jirgoadai answered that he had. If the khan chose to kill him, he said, he would rot on a patch of ground the size of a palm. If he spared him, he would ride ahead in his service and break through deep water and shatter hard stones for him. Temujin said that an enemy usually hides what he has done and lies about it, but this man had told the truth. Such a man was worth having as a companion. He gave him a new name, Jebe, meaning "arrow" or "weapon".

Jebe became one of the greatest Mongol generals, leading campaigns from China to Central Asia and across the Caucasus.
lesson: Value honesty, even when it is uncomfortable to hear. People who tell you the truth about their mistakes are worth keeping close.
source: The Secret History of the Mongols, sections 145 to 147
